# Evidence Library screening + synthesis (v2)

You screen sports-science PDFs and, if eligible, write a library record for Baylor Athletics performance, medical, rehab, nutrition and research staff.

Inputs: `inputs.json` gives each paper an ID, the filename it was catalogued under (`sourceFile`), page count, and DOI strings found anywhere in the text (`doiCandidatesInText`; most are from the reference list). Full extracted text is at `text/<ID>.txt`. Read it fully, in chunks if large. Controlled vocabularies are in `taxonomy.json`. Use ONLY those exact values. Base everything ONLY on the extracted text, never on outside knowledge of the paper.

## Decision
- `INCLUDE`: the text is the article the filename names, AND it is athlete health/performance evidence of one of these types: original research (any design, including case reports and validation studies), systematic review/meta-analysis, narrative or clinical review, or consensus/position statement.
- `EXCLUDE` (give `exclusionReason`):
  - (a) source identity mismatch: the text is a different article from what the filename names. Compare the filename title with the title in the text carefully.
  - (b) editorial, commentary, letter, or opinion piece without original methods or a structured review of evidence. Also (b): a study protocol with no results (decided by Eric 2026-10-10; no listed reason fits exactly, so use (b) and say "study protocol, no results" in the reason).
  - (c) not relevant to athletes, sport, exercise performance or athlete health.
- `DEGRADED` (give `degradedReason`): the text is unreadable or truncated, critical sections are missing, or **the article's own DOI is not printed in the text**. Reference-list DOIs do not count. If the DOI is missing but everything else is fine, still fill in all fields and set `doiMissing: true`. The operator may verify the DOI externally and upgrade the decision.

## Output: write `drafts/<ID>.json`
```
{
 "id":"<ID>", "sourceFile":"...", "decision":"INCLUDE|EXCLUDE|DEGRADED",
 "exclusionReason":"", "degradedReason":"", "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"one sentence: title found in text vs filename",
 "confidence":"high|medium|low",
 "studyDesign":"<one studyDesigns value>",
 "primaryDomain":"<one domains value>", "domains":[...must include primaryDomain], "audiences":[...], "sports":[...], "populations":[...],
 "evidenceSummary":"2-3 sentences: design, sample, main results, as the authors report them",
 "screeningLimitations":"1-2 sentences: key limits on what this evidence can support",
 "synthesisCaution":"1 sentence: the most likely way staff could over-read this paper",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020, "citation":"Authors. Title. Journal. Year;vol(issue):pages.", "doi":"10.xxxx/...",
   "abstract":"", "tldr":"", "methods":"", "findings":"", "limitations":"",
   "practicalImplications":"", "athleteDev":"", "rtp":""
 }
}
```
For EXCLUDE, the taxonomy, summary and `paper` fields may be null.

## Field rules
- `year`: the journal issue/publication year from the citation line or the journal header. NOT the received, accepted or online-first date. If only an online-first date exists, use that year.
- `doi`: the article's own DOI, exactly as printed, lowercase prefix "10.". Never use a DOI from the references.
- `citation`: list authors as printed (surname + initials; use "et al." after 6 authors). Include volume, issue and pages only if they are printed for this article. Do not invent them.
- `populations`: add `Male Athletes` and/or `Female Athletes` when the sample is athletes and their sex is stated. Do not use athlete tags (sex or `Healthy Athletes`) for non-athlete samples such as recreationally active adults, patients, staff or students; use `Adult / Recreational` or `Mixed / Unspecified`. Add `Healthy Athletes` or `Injured Athletes` when health status is stated. Add the competition level (Professional / Elite, Collegiate, Youth / Adolescent, Adult / Recreational). Use `Mixed / Unspecified` only when the level really is mixed or unstated.
- `studyDesign`: code scoping reviews with a described systematic search as `Systematic Review / Meta-analysis` (library precedent). Use `Narrative Review` only when no search method is described.
- `primaryDomain`: the domain staff would browse to find this paper. Use Monitoring & Technology for papers whose main contribution is a measurement tool, test, device or monitoring method, including reliability, validity and test profiling.
- If the abstract and the results/tables disagree, report the results/table values and note the conflict in `limitations`.

## Writing standard (critical)
- Every claim must be directly supported by the text. Report sample sizes, designs, effect directions and significance accurately. Never invent numbers.
- Distinguish within-group change from between-group difference. Distinguish association from causation. Do not overstate observational or small-sample findings.
- Each paper field: 1-3 plain sentences. `tldr`: one or two practitioner sentences. `athleteDev` = Performance Application. `rtp` = Return to Sport Application. If the study cannot inform return to sport, say what it cannot be used for.
- Practical fields must follow from the findings. No generic advice the paper does not support.
- Plain language, no em dashes.

 "evidenceSummary": "Randomized repeated-measures laboratory study of 11 male athletes (lacrosse, soccer, rugby and football) who completed four agility circuits on two outdoor fields with different mechanical properties, tested 7 days apart. Energy return was lower on Field A (28.2%) than Field B (41.6%); summed surface EMG was higher on the lower-return field (P = .026) and agility circuits took longer there, while metabolic measures did not differ significantly between fields.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only two fields, one shoe type and 11 men were tested, and no injury outcomes were measured. The abstract says muscle activity was '<13%' on the lower-return field, but the results report it as 13% greater there, so the direction should be checked against the tables.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the 'unfamiliar fields may cause overuse' idea as an established injury mechanism, but the study measured EMG and gas exchange in healthy men on two fields and did not measure injury.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2018,
  "citation": "Hales ME, Johnson JD II. The Influence of Sport-Field Properties on Muscle-Recruitment Patterns and Metabolic Response. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018 (ahead of print).",
  "doi": "10.1123/ijspp.2018-0004",
  "abstract": "Eleven male athletes completed four agility circuits on two outdoor fields with different mechanical properties. Surface EMG, gas exchange, and 30-m sprint times were recorded before and after the circuits. The authors report that muscle activity differed between fields and that the field with greater energy return gave faster agility and sprint times, with largely similar metabolic responses.",
  "tldr": "The surface a player trains on changed how 11 male athletes recruited their leg muscles during agility work. The lower energy-return field produced more muscle activity and slower agility times, so surface mechanics are worth considering in conditioning.",
  "methods": "Eleven male athletes completed four consecutive agility circuits with 60 s rests on two outdoor fields, tested 7 days apart at the same time of day. Surface EMG was recorded from the vastus medialis, biceps femoris, gastrocnemius medial head and tibialis anterior, with a portable gas analyser for VO2, HR and energy expenditure. Field properties were measured with the ASTM F-1936 protocol, and 30-m sprints were run before and after the circuits.",
  "findings": "Energy restitution was lower on Field A (28.2%) than Field B (41.6%), and force reduction and vertical deformation were also different. Summed muscle activity was significantly different between fields (F(1,20) = 5.78, P = .026), with about 13% more activity on the lower-return field, and agility circuits took longer there (P = .02). Pretest 30-m sprints were slower on Field A (4.67 vs 4.31 s). Metabolic variables changed across trials but did not differ significantly between fields.",
  "limitations": "Only 11 men and two fields were tested, with no injury outcomes, and the fatigue correlations were weak (r = 0.28 to 0.42). The abstract and results disagree on the direction of the EMG difference (<13% vs 13% greater on the lower-return field).",
  "practicalImplications": "Player development staff should consider a field's energy return and shock absorption when planning conditioning and training volume. Preparing athletes on a surface with similar mechanical properties to the competition surface is a reasonable approach, according to the authors.",
  "athleteDev": "Where possible, prepare athletes on surfaces that resemble the competition surface, and plan drills and volume knowing that energy return changes muscle activity and agility times. The study does not show that any specific footwear or training change improves performance.",
  "rtp": "This study tested healthy athletes only and does not inform return-to-sport decisions or the timing of return after injury."
 }
}

     The Inﬂuence of Sport-Field Properties on Muscle-Recruitment
                  Patterns and Metabolic Response
                                                   Michael E. Hales and John D. Johnson II

     Purpose: To investigate different sport-ﬁeld properties’ inﬂuence on muscle-recruitment patterns and metabolic response
     during a series of running and agility drills. Methods: Eleven male athletes were ﬁtted with a standard multipurpose training
     shoe. The test protocol consisting of 4 high-intensity trials with 60-s rests between trials performed on 2 ﬁelds with different
     properties. Time-dependent ﬁeld properties were measured using the American Standards for Testing and Materials
     protocol (F-1936). A 30-m pretest and posttest sprint determined fatigue and player performance. Electromyography
     (EMG) recorded muscle activity for vastus medialis, biceps femoris, gastrocnemius medial head, and tibialis anterior, and
     metabolic activity analyzed maximal oxygen consumption, heart rate, respiratory exchange ratio, metabolic equivalent, and
     energy expenditure. Results: A difference was calculated for muscle activity across trials (P = .01) for both surfaces. Muscle
     activity was <13% on the ﬁeld with less energy return (P = .01). Metabolic components (maximal oxygen consumption,
     heart rate, respiratory exchange ratio, metabolic equivalent, and energy expenditure) were signiﬁcantly different across
     trials (P = .01) but not signiﬁcantly different between ﬁelds. The participants completed the agility course (5.2%) faster on
     the ﬁeld with greater energy return, while caloric expenditure was similar between ﬁelds. Conclusions: The ﬁndings
     indicate that ﬁeld mechanical properties inﬂuence muscle-activation patterns. The ﬁeld demonstrating the greatest
     magnitude of energy return produces the lowest sprint and agility course times; however, performing on a ﬁeld exhibiting
     unfamiliar mechanical properties could cause the athlete to produce atypical movement patterns that might contribute to
     overuse of the neuromuscular system.

     Keywords: neuromuscular, electromyography, metabolism, fatigue, energy return

 "evidenceSummary": "Randomized repeated-measures laboratory study of 11 male athletes (lacrosse, soccer, rugby and football) who completed four agility circuits on two outdoor fields with different mechanical properties, tested 7 days apart. Energy return was lower on Field A (28.2%) than Field B (41.6%); summed surface EMG was higher on the lower-return field (P = .026) and agility circuits took longer there, while metabolic measures did not differ significantly between fields overall.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only two fields, one shoe type and 11 men were tested, and no injury outcomes were measured. The size of the EMG difference is reported inconsistently: the abstract says '<13%', the discussion says 13% greater, and the Table 2 means are about 30% higher on the lower-return field.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the 'unfamiliar fields may cause overuse' idea as an established injury mechanism, but the study measured EMG and gas exchange in healthy men on two fields and did not measure injury.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2018,
  "citation": "Hales ME, Johnson JD II. The Influence of Sport-Field Properties on Muscle-Recruitment Patterns and Metabolic Response. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018 (ahead of print).",
  "doi": "10.1123/ijspp.2018-0004",
  "abstract": "Eleven male athletes completed four agility circuits on two outdoor fields with different mechanical properties. Surface EMG, gas exchange, and 30-m sprint times were recorded before and after the circuits. The authors report that muscle activity differed between fields and that the field with greater energy return gave faster agility and sprint times, with largely similar metabolic responses.",
  "tldr": "The surface a player trains on changed how 11 male athletes recruited their leg muscles during agility work. The lower energy-return field produced more muscle activity and slower agility times, so surface mechanics are worth considering in conditioning.",
  "methods": "Eleven male athletes completed four consecutive agility circuits with 60 s rests on two outdoor fields, tested 7 days apart at the same time of day. Surface EMG was recorded from the vastus medialis, biceps femoris, gastrocnemius medial head and tibialis anterior, with a portable gas analyser for VO2, HR and energy expenditure. Field properties were measured with the ASTM F-1936 protocol, and 30-m sprints were run before and after the circuits.",
  "findings": "Energy restitution was lower on Field A (28.2%) than Field B (41.6%), and force reduction and vertical deformation also differed. Summed muscle activity differed between fields (F(1,20) = 5.78, P = .026) and was higher on Field A in every trial (Table 2, for example T1 740.8 vs 566.6), and agility circuits took longer there (P = .02). Pretest 30-m sprints were slower on Field A (4.67 vs 4.31 s), and metabolic variables changed across trials but did not differ significantly between fields overall.",
  "limitations": "Only 11 men and two fields were tested, with no injury outcomes, and the fatigue correlations were weak to moderate (r = .28 to .42). The EMG difference is reported as '<13%' in the abstract and 13% greater in the discussion, but the Table 2 means are about 30% higher on Field A. The field effect was analysed with field as a between-subject factor (F(1,20)) even though the same athletes ran on both fields.",
  "practicalImplications": "The authors recommend that player development staff consider a field's energy return and shock absorption when planning conditioning and training volume. They suggest preparing athletes on a surface with mechanical properties similar to the competition surface.",
  "athleteDev": "Where possible, prepare athletes on surfaces that resemble the competition surface, and plan drills and volume knowing that energy return changes muscle activity and agility times. The study does not show that any specific footwear or training change improves performance.",
  "rtp": "This study tested healthy athletes only and does not inform return-to-sport decisions or the timing of return after injury."
 },

   "screeningLimitations and paper.limitations: added that Table 2 shows about a 30% difference, not 13%, and that field was analysed as a between-subject factor ('1 between-subject independent variable (field type)')",
   "paper.limitations: correlations 'weak (r = 0.28 to 0.42)' -> weak to moderate ('A moderate correlation ... TA muscle activity (r = .421')",
   "paper.practicalImplications: attributed both recommendations to the authors ('Player development professionals should consider the mechanical properties')"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "Field descriptions are internally inconsistent: Field A has lower force reduction and vertical deformation (stiffer by those measures) yet Figure 3 calls it the field with 'greater absorption properties'.   "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q02",
 "sourceFile": "The Influence of Time of Season on Injury Rates and the Epidemiology of Canadian Football Injuries.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'The Influence of Time of Season on Injury Rates and the Epidemiology of Canadian Football Injuries' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": [
  "Sports Medicine & Injury"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Sports Medicine",
  "Athletic Training"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "American Football"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Professional / Elite"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Prospective cohort analysis of routinely collected injury surveillance data from eight Canadian Football League seasons (2011 to 2018). Game medical-attention injuries occurred at 45.2 per 100 athletes at risk and time-loss game injuries at 30.7 per 100, with weekly rates falling about 1% per week over the season and about 30% in the playoffs compared with preseason. The number of ongoing time-loss injuries rose during the regular season.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Observational data from one professional league, relying on staff and player reporting, with no practice exposure denominators. The study shows patterns across the season but cannot explain why rates change.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the small weekly decline as a reason to reduce injury prevention late in the season, but the drop is small, and the playoff fall may reflect fewer teams playing or less reporting, which the authors could not test.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2020,
  "citation": "Robbins SM, Bodnar C, Donatien P, Mirza R, Zhao ZY, et al. The Influence of Time of Season on Injury Rates and the Epidemiology of Canadian Football Injuries. Clin J Sport Med 2020;00:1-7.",
  "doi": "10.1097/JSM.0000000000000824",
  "abstract": "Prospective cohort study using eight seasons of Canadian Football League injury surveillance data. Medical-attention and time-loss injury rates were analysed by week of season, player position, injury type and anatomical location, and the burden of ongoing time-loss injuries was tracked across the season.",
  "tldr": "In the CFL, injury rates fell slightly through the season (about 1% per week) and dropped further in the playoffs. Ongoing time-loss injuries built up during the regular season, so medical workload may rise late in the year.",
  "methods": "Routinely collected CFL surveillance data from 2011 to 2018 were analysed with Poisson regression, with athletes at risk as the offset. Game injury rates are expressed per 100 athletes at risk; practice injuries are reported as counts only because the number of players at practice was not recorded. Injury burden was the number of players with an uncleared time-loss injury in a given week.",
  "findings": "The game medical-attention rate was 45.2 per 100 athletes at risk and the time-loss game rate was 30.7 per 100. Weekly rates declined about 1% per week across the season (rate ratio 0.99), and time-loss rates in the playoffs were lower than in preseason (rate ratio 0.70). Quarterbacks, offensive backs and linebackers had the highest game injury rates, and joint/ligament injuries were the most common game injury type.",
  "limitations": "Injury data depended on information from players and medical staff, so underreporting is possible. Practice injury rates could not be calculated, and every injury was counted separately, so repeat injuries to one athlete count the same as injuries to different athletes.",
  "practicalImplications": "Medical staff can plan for a rise in ongoing time-loss injuries as the regular season progresses, and for lower new-injury rates in the playoffs. Quarterbacks, offensive backs and linebackers had the highest game injury rates in this dataset and may warrant closer monitoring.",
  "athleteDev": "Position-specific game injury rates can help set priorities for monitoring in a professional football setting, with the highest-rate positions first. The rates describe injuries in one league, so they should not be used to set training loads.",
  "rtp": "The study describes injury rates and ongoing time-loss burden across a season. It does not measure recovery times for specific injuries or return-to-play decisions, so it cannot inform when an individual player should return."
 }
}

The Influence of Time of Season on Injury Rates and
the Epidemiology of Canadian Football Injuries
Shawn M. Robbins, BScPT, PhD,*† Camille Bodnar, MScPT,* Pierre Donatien, MScPT,* Rabia Mirza, MScPT,*
Zhen Yuan Zhao, MScPT,* Shane Hoeber, MD,‡ Dhiren Naidu, MD,‡ Annabelle Redelmeier, MSc,§
Russell J. Steele, PhD,{ and Ian Shrier, MD, PhD║


  Abstract
  Objective: To describe injury rates and injury patterns in the Canadian Football League (CFL) according to time during the season,
  player position, injury type, and injury location. Design: Prospective, cohort study. Setting and Participants: Eight seasons
  from CFL injury surveillance database. Independent Variables: Depending on the analysis, time of season (preseason, regular,
  and playoffs), player position, injury type, and injury location. Main Outcome Measures: Medical attention and time-loss injury
  rates per 100 athletes at risk (AAR), and prevalence of time-loss injuries per week. Results: The average game injury rate was 45.2/
  100 AAR medical attention injuries and 30.7/100 AAR time-loss injuries. Injury rates declined by 1% per week over the season for
  both medical attention (rate ratio 5 0.99) and time-loss (rate ratio 5 0.99) injuries, with a substantial decline during the playoffs
  compared with preseason (rate ratio 5 0.70-0.77). The number of ongoing time-loss injuries increased over the course of the regular
  season. Quarterbacks, offensive backs, and linebackers had the highest game injury rates. Joint/ligament and muscle/tendon
  injuries were the most common injury types for games and practices, respectively. The lower extremity was the most commonly
  affected area, specifically the lower leg/ankle/foot and hip/groin/thigh. Conclusions: There was a 1% decline in injury rate per
  week during the season and a 30% decline during the playoffs. The number of ongoing time-loss injuries increased over the regular
  season. Current results can aid league officials and medical staff in making evidence-based decisions concerning player safety and
  health.
  Key Words: Canadian Football League, football, injury rate
  (Clin J Sport Med 2020;00:1–7)

The authors conclude that caffeine acutely increases maximal strength, muscular endurance and power, and that doses of 3 to 9 mg per kg taken about 60 minutes before exercise seem adequate.",
 "screeningLimitations": "As a narrative review without a described search, the study selection cannot be reproduced. Most included trials are small and mostly male, and many did not check whether participants were blinded, which limits how far the dose and sex-specific advice applies.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could apply the 3 to 9 mg per kg dose and strength gains to competitive lifters or female athletes, but the review says that trained athletes and women are under-studied.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2018,
  "citation": "Grgic J, Mikulic P, Schoenfeld BJ, Bishop DJ, Pedisic Z. The Influence of Caffeine Supplementation on Resistance Exercise: A Review. Sports Med. 2018.",
  "doi": "10.1007/s40279-018-0997-y",
  "abstract": "A review that critically evaluates the evidence on caffeine supplementation before resistance exercise and gives practical guidelines on dosing. It covers maximal strength, muscular endurance, power, perceived exertion, pain, muscle damage, hormones, blood pressure, caffeine form, habitual intake, timing, genetics and placebo effects.",
  "tldr": "Caffeine appears to acutely raise maximal strength, muscular endurance and power in resistance exercise, and doses of 3 to 9 mg per kg about 60 minutes before exercise look adequate. It can raise blood pressure, so people with high blood pressure need caution.",
  "methods": "Narrative review of the caffeine and resistance exercise literature, covering 1RM, isometric and isokinetic strength, muscular endurance, power, delayed-onset muscle soreness, muscle damage, hormonal and cardiovascular responses, dose, timing, caffeine form and genetics. The authors draw on earlier meta-analyses, and no systematic search method is described.",
  "findings": "The authors report that caffeine increases 1RM and MVC strength and muscular endurance, and enhances power, with effects that may depend on dose and external load. Effects on perceived exertion and pain perception are inconsistent, and there is preliminary evidence that caffeine can reduce soreness. Caffeine acutely increases systolic blood pressure in several studies, while the hormone increases are of questionable practical significance.",
  "limitations": "The review is narrative, and most of the underlying studies have small samples, are mostly in men, and often include untrained or recreationally trained participants. Placebo effects and blinding are a concern, and the authors call for research in women, competitive powerlifters and weightlifters, and long-term adaptation.",
  "practicalImplications": "The authors suggest starting with a lower dose such as 3 mg per kg taken about 60 minutes before exercise, then adjusting to the individual. Athletes in power-dominated events may consider caffeine before training, and caution is advised for people with high blood pressure.",
  "athleteDev": "For strength and power sessions, a pre-session caffeine dose of about 3 to 9 mg per kg taken about 60 minutes before training may help, starting low and adjusting to the athlete's response. Evidence in trained athletes is thin because most studies used untrained or recreationally trained men.",
  "rtp": "This review does not study injured athletes or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Its blood pressure findings are relevant to health screening rather than rehabilitation."
 }

    REVIEW ARTICLE



The Influence of Caffeine Supplementation on Resistance Exercise:
A Review
Jozo Grgic1 · Pavle Mikulic2 · Brad J. Schoenfeld3 · David J. Bishop1,4 · Zeljko Pedisic1


© Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2018


Abstract
This paper aims to critically evaluate and thoroughly discuss the evidence on the topic of caffeine supplementation when
performing resistance exercise, as well as provide practical guidelines for the ingestion of caffeine prior to resistance
exercise. Based on the current evidence, it seems that caffeine increases both maximal strength and muscular endurance.
Furthermore, power appears to be enhanced with caffeine supplementation, although this effect might, to a certain extent,
be caffeine dose- and external load-dependent. A reduction in rating of perceived exertion (RPE) might contribute to the
performance-enhancing effects of caffeine supplementation as some studies have observed decreases in RPE coupled with
increases in performance following caffeine ingestion. However, the same does not seem to be the case for pain perception
as there is evidence showing acute increases in resistance exercise performance without any significant effects of caffeine
ingestion on pain perception. Some studies have reported that caffeine ingestion did not affect exercise-induced muscle dam-
age, but that it might reduce perceived resistance exercise-induced delayed-onset muscle soreness; however, this needs to be
explored further. There is some evidence that caffeine ingestion, compared with a placebo, may lead to greater increases in
the production of testosterone and cortisol following resistance exercise. However, given that the acute changes in hormone
levels seem to be weakly correlated with hallmark adaptations to resistance exercise, such as hypertrophy and increased
muscular strength, these findings are likely of questionable practical significance. Although not without contrasting findings,
the available evidence suggests that caffeine ingestion can lead to acute increases in blood pressure (primarily systolic), and
thus caution is needed regarding caffeine supplementation among individuals with high blood pressure. In the vast majority
of studies, caffeine was administered in capsule or powder forms, and therefore the effects of alternative forms of caffeine,
such as chewing gums or mouth rinses, on resistance exercise performance remain unclear. The emerging evidence suggests
that coffee might be at least equally ergogenic as caffeine alone when the caffeine dose is matched. Doses in the range of
3–9 mg·kg−1 seem to be adequate for eliciting an ergogenic effect when administered 60 min pre-exercise. In general, caffeine
seems to be safe when taken in the recommended doses. However, at doses as high as 9 mg·kg−1 or higher, side effects such
as insomnia might be more pronounced. It remains unclear whether habituation reduces the ergogenic benefits of caffeine
on resistance exercise as no evidence exists for this type of exercise. Caution is needed when extrapolating these conclusions
to females as the vast majority of studies involved only male participants.

 "evidenceSummary": "Test-retest and concordance study of 20 healthy male volunteers who trained upper-limb sports about 8 hours per week. The handheld-dynamometer version agreed well with the force plate version (ICC 0.864 to 0.952, no significant paired difference), and inter-session reliability was moderate to good (ICC 0.643 to 0.923), best in the I position.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Only 20 healthy men playing mixed upper-limb sports were tested, with reliability measured one week apart. The findings establish agreement and reliability in healthy athletes, not validity against injury, fatigue or return to play.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the modified test as a validated return-to-play or fatigue measure, but this study assessed agreement and reliability in healthy athletes only.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2022,
  "citation": "Tooth C, Forthomme B, Croisier JL, Gofflot A, Bornheim S, Schwartz C. The Modified-Athletic Shoulder Test: Reliability and validity of a new on-field assessment tool. Phys Ther Sport. 2022;58:8-15.",
  "doi": "10.1016/j.ptsp.2022.08.003",
  "abstract": "Twenty healthy male athletes who played upper-limb sports performed the Athletic Shoulder Test on a force plate and a modified version using a handheld dynamometer, in two sessions seven days apart. Concordance and inter-session reliability were assessed in three arm positions, and scapular muscle EMG was recorded during the tests.",
  "tldr": "The handheld-dynamometer version of the Athletic Shoulder Test agreed well with the force plate version in healthy upper-limb athletes, and the I position was the most reliable. Athletes should be familiarised with the test first, because strength was higher in the second session.",
  "methods": "Test-retest and concordance study of 20 healthy male volunteers with a mean age of about 22 years who trained upper-limb sports about 8 hours per week. Isometric shoulder strength was measured in the I, Y and T positions with a force plate and a handheld dynamometer, in two sessions seven days apart. Upper trapezius, lower trapezius and serratus anterior EMG was recorded during the first session. Reliability was assessed with ICC, SEM, MDC95, paired t tests and Bland-Altman plots.",
  "findings": "Concordance between the two tools was good to excellent (ICC 0.864 to 0.952) with no significant paired difference in any position. Inter-session reliability of the handheld version was moderate to good (ICC 0.643 to 0.923), with the I position most reliable (ICC 0.923); the MDC95 was about 39% of the mean in the Y position. Peak strength was 4 to 10% higher in the second session, significantly so for all positions with the force plate but only for the Y position with the handheld dynamometer.",
  "limitations": "The sample was 20 men from mixed upper-limb sports, with no injured athletes, and EMG was measured only in the first session before familiarisation. The abstract gives a concordance ICC range of 0.86 to 0.97, whereas the results report 0.864 to 0.952, and some confidence intervals are wide (for example 0.233 to 0.849 for the Y position).",
  "practicalImplications": "A handheld dynamometer can be used on the field to repeat isometric shoulder strength measures, with the I position the most reliable if only one position can be tested. Familiarisation trials should be given before testing, and results from the Y position need caution because of high variability.",
  "athleteDev": "Staff can use the handheld version to track isometric shoulder strength in overhead athletes, using the I position and a familiarisation session first. Interpret changes in the Y position cautiously, because day-to-day variability is large.",
  "rtp": "The study tested healthy athletes only and did not compare the test with injury, surgery or return-to-play outcomes. It should not be used as a return-to-play decision tool on the basis of this study alone."
 }
}

19 August 2022
                                                          Setting: University Motion Lab.
Accepted 22 August 2022
                                                          Participants: Twenty healthy volunteers who practiced an upper limb sport for at least 5 h per week
                                                          were recruited for the study.
Keywords:
                                                          Main outcome measures: The concordance between the Athletic Shoulder Test (AST) and the Modiﬁed-
strength
functional testing
                                                          Athletic Shoulder Test (M-AST) was assessed with intra-class correlation coefﬁcients (ICC), paired T-
upper limb athlete                                        Test and Bland-Altman plots. The inter-session reliability was assessed with intra-class correlation co-
                                                          efﬁcients (ICC), SEM, MDC and paired T-Test.
                                                          Results: A strong concordance was found between AST and M-AST values (ICC ¼ 0.86e0.97; p > 0.05) in
                                                          all the positions considered and for both sessions. Bland-Altman plots conﬁrmed these results. However,
                                                          the inter-session reliability was more variable for both AST and M-AST (ICC ¼ 0.643e0.923; p < 0.05).
                                                          Conclusions: The M-AST seems to be a reliable, cheaper and easier to implement alternative to the AST to
                                                          measure recovery status following matches or training sessions in upper limb athletes. As for the AST,
                                                          familiarization trials will have to be performed before the assessment to have accurate measurements.
                                                          Clinical trials registration number: NCT05112380.

  "athleteDev": "Use the mechanistic picture as background for training design rather than as a fixed prescription, since endurance adaptation is better characterised than resistance adaptation and individual response varies. Avoid compounds marketed as exercise mimetics, because human performance evidence for them is absent.",
  "rtp": "The review covers training adaptation in healthy and elite athletes and does not study injured athletes or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Rehabilitation is mentioned only in passing."

}

                                                                                                                            REVIEW ARTICLE


THE MOLECULAR ATHLETE: EXERCISE
PHYSIOLOGY FROM MECHANISMS TO MEDALS
                                                                                      AUTHORS
                                                                                      Regula Furrer, John A. Hawley,
                                                                                      Christoph Handschin



                                                                                      CORRESPONDENCE
                                                                                      christoph.handschin@unibas.ch;
                                                                                      regula.furrer@unibas.ch;
                                                                                      john.hawley@acu.edu.au



                                                                                      KEY WORDS
                                                                                      athlete; endurance training; exercise; resistance
                                                                                      training; skeletal muscle



CLINICAL HIGHLIGHTS
   1)   During human evolution, Homo sapiens emerged as mobile hunters and gatherers, dependent on the natural avail-
        ability of food. However, today’s sedentary lifestyle and overabundant food availability place a major burden on our
        metabolic health and are strong drivers underpinning the dramatic rise  . in noncommunicable diseases.
  2)    A sedentary lifestyle, characterized by low maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max), unfavorable body composition, and low
        muscle strength, is an independent risk factor for many chronic diseases and a strong predictor of morbidity and mor-
        tality.
  3)    Despite marked interindividual differences in the response to standardized exercise training, regular physical activity
        lowers the risk of and confers therapeutic beneﬁts for many noncommunicable diseases.
  4)    Endurance- and resistance-based exercise training protocols confer distinct clinical and health-related beneﬁts and
        can prevent or reverse many lifestyle-induced metabolic diseases.
  5)    Clinical exercise tests based on established, validated physiological outcomes are essential for the diagnosis and
        subsequent monitoring of clinical conditions.
  6)    Investigations of elite human performance provide valuable insights into the molecular, cellular, tissue, and whole
        body adaptations to extreme metabolic loading. Identiﬁcation of the mechanisms and pathways that limit exercise
        capacity may ultimately aid in the identiﬁcation of novel therapeutic targets to be prescribed to patient populations.

THE MOLECULAR ATHLETE: EXERCISE
PHYSIOLOGY FROM MECHANISMS TO MEDALS
    Regula Furrer,1   John A. Hawley,2 and   Christoph Handschin1
1
 Biozentrum, University of Basel, Basel, Switzerland and 2Exercise and Nutrition Research Program, Mary MacKillop Institute for
Health Research, Australian Catholic University, Melbourne, Victoria, Australia


         Abstract
         Human skeletal muscle demonstrates remarkable plasticity, adapting to numerous external stimuli including the
         habitual level of contractile loading. Accordingly, muscle function and exercise capacity encompass a broad spec-
         trum, from inactive individuals with low levels of endurance and strength to elite athletes who produce prodigious
         performances underpinned by pleiotropic training-induced muscular adaptations. Our current understanding of the
         signal integration, interpretation, and output coordination of the cellular and molecular mechanisms that govern
         muscle plasticity across this continuum is incomplete. As such, training methods and their application to elite ath-
         letes largely rely on a “trial-and-error” approach, with the experience and practices of successful coaches and ath-
         letes often providing the bases for “post hoc” scientiﬁc enquiry and research. This review provides a synopsis of
         the morphological and functional changes along with the molecular mechanisms underlying exercise adaptation to
         endurance- and resistance-based training. These traits are placed in the context of innate genetic and interindivid-
         ual differences in exercise capacity and performance, with special consideration given to aging athletes.
         Collectively, we provide a comprehensive overview of skeletal muscle plasticity in response to different modes of
         exercise and how such adaptations translate from “molecules to medals.”

  "abstract": "A review of dietary and non-dietary factors that modify the muscle protein synthetic response to feeding after resistance-type exercise. Alcohol, energy restriction and excess body fat reduce the response, while a higher protein intake can offset some of the reduction during energy restriction.",
  "limitations": "Most evidence comes from isolated protein drinks given over 4 to 5 hours, mostly in young men, so transfer to mixed meals, longer periods, women and older athletes is uncertain. Only one study has measured muscle protein synthesis after a mixed meal, and synthesis is a short-term marker that does not always match changes in muscle mass.",
  "practicalImplications": "A practical per-meal target after resistance exercise is about 20 g of high-quality, fast-digesting protein. Slower proteins or long gaps before the next meal may call for 40 g or more, and the authors suggest older athletes aim for about 30 g per meal. Binge drinking and high-dose antioxidant supplements should be avoided around training.",
  "athleteDev": "After resistance sessions, about 20 g of high-quality protein gives a near-maximal response, and slower proteins such as casein may need 40 g or more if the next meal is six or more hours away. Limit binge drinking around training, because alcohol blunts the response to protein.",
  "rtp": "This review concerns healthy, mainly young adults after resistance exercise and does not study injured athletes or return to sport. The authors note that disuse and lower intake can reduce the protein response, but this was not tested in injured athletes."
 }
}

    REVIEW ARTICLE



The Muscle Protein Synthetic Response to Meal Ingestion Following
Resistance‑Type Exercise
Jorn Trommelen1 · Milan W. Betz1 · Luc J. C. van Loon1


© The Author(s) 2019


Abstract
Protein ingestion following resistance-type exercise stimulates muscle protein synthesis rates and consequently enhances the
skeletal muscle adaptive response to prolonged training. Ingestion of ~ 20 g of quickly digestible protein isolate optimizes
muscle protein synthesis rates during the first few hours of post-exercise recovery. However, the majority of daily protein
intake is consumed as slower digestible, nutrient-rich, whole-food protein sources as part of mixed meals. Therefore, the
muscle protein synthetic response to the ingestion of protein supplements and typical foods or mixed meals may differ sub-
stantially. In addition, the muscle protein synthetic response to feeding is not only determined by acute nutrient intake but is
also likely modulated by habitual energy and nutrient intake and nondietary factors such as habitual physical activity, body
composition, age, and/or sex. Therefore, nutritional recommendations to maximize the muscle protein synthetic response to
exercise depend on the type of meal (e.g., protein supplements vs. mixed meals) and the time until the next feeding oppor-
tunity (e.g., feeding before overnight sleep) and, therefore, need to be personalized to the individual athlete.

    REVIEW ARTICLE



The Muscle Protein Synthetic Response to Meal Ingestion Following
Resistance‑Type Exercise
Jorn Trommelen1 · Milan W. Betz1 · Luc J. C. van Loon1


© The Author(s) 2019


Abstract
Protein ingestion following resistance-type exercise stimulates muscle protein synthesis rates and consequently enhances the
skeletal muscle adaptive response to prolonged training. Ingestion of ~ 20 g of quickly digestible protein isolate optimizes
muscle protein synthesis rates during the first few hours of post-exercise recovery. However, the majority of daily protein
intake is consumed as slower digestible, nutrient-rich, whole-food protein sources as part of mixed meals. Therefore, the
muscle protein synthetic response to the ingestion of protein supplements and typical foods or mixed meals may differ sub-
stantially. In addition, the muscle protein synthetic response to feeding is not only determined by acute nutrient intake but is
also likely modulated by habitual energy and nutrient intake and nondietary factors such as habitual physical activity, body
composition, age, and/or sex. Therefore, nutritional recommendations to maximize the muscle protein synthetic response to
exercise depend on the type of meal (e.g., protein supplements vs. mixed meals) and the time until the next feeding oppor-
tunity (e.g., feeding before overnight sleep) and, therefore, need to be personalized to the individual athlete.

 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read 'vmax matters most' as proof that top-speed training improves game speed or that acceleration work can be dropped; the study covers combine-style 36.6 m times only.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2019,
  "citation": "Clark KP, Rieger RH, Bruno RF, Stearne DJ. The NFL Combine 40-yard dash: how important is maximum velocity? J Strength Cond Res. 2019;33(6):1542-1550.",
  "doi": "",
  "abstract": "Publicly available 2016 NFL Combine split times were fitted with a velocity-profile model to estimate maximum velocity and acceleration patterns for 260 players. The authors examined how maximum velocity related to sprint performance and whether fast and slow groups accelerated in a similar way relative to their top speed.",
  "tldr": "In the 40-yard dash, top speed tracks overall sprint time closely, and players of different speeds accelerate in a similar way relative to their own top speed. Preparation for combine-style sprints may need more top-speed work.",
  "methods": "Secondary analysis of 260 players' 2016 NFL Combine split times from three public websites. A monoexponential velocity model was fitted to each athlete's 9.1, 18.3 and 36.6 m times to derive vmax and t, and the group was split into fast and slow halves by vmax for independent t tests and effect sizes.",
  "findings": "Modelled times matched measured times closely (mean absolute error below 0.03 s). vmax correlated strongly with split times (r2 0.72, 0.83 and 0.94 for 9.1, 18.3 and 36.6 m). The t values did not differ between fast and slow groups (0.768 vs 0.773 s; d = 0.08, trivial), and both groups reached about 90% of vmax by 13.7 m.",
  "limitations": "The analysis used one combine's publicly posted times, and players were analysed as one group without adjustment for position or mass. The authors note that correlation does not show that vmax causes faster acceleration, and that their t values were lower than earlier studies, which they attribute to the automatic timing start.",
  "practicalImplications": "The authors suggest that maximum velocity is more closely related to short sprint performance than previously recognised, so combine preparation may warrant more top-speed work. They also suggest a flying 18.3 m sprint with automatic timing gates can estimate vmax closely.",
  "athleteDev": "For 40-yard dash preparation, include top-speed work, and consider a flying 18.3 m sprint with timing gates to estimate vmax and check whether split times are on track. The study does not show that top-speed training improves in-game speed.",
  "rtp": "The study concerns healthy draft-age players in a combine test and includes no injury or return-to-play data, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions."

  "tldr": "Most NFL players (79%) returned to play after common orthopaedic surgery, but patellar tendon repair had the lowest return rate (50%). ACL reconstruction and patellar tendon repair were followed by shorter careers and lasting drops in performance.",
  "methods": "Retrospective case series of 559 NFL athletes who were on an active roster or injured reserve at the time of surgery, confirmed by two sources. Return to play was defined as at least one regular-season game after surgery, and a position-specific performance score was compared with the season before injury. Offensive linemen and special teams players were excluded from the performance analysis, and procedures with fewer than 25 cases were excluded.",
  "findings": "Overall return to play was 79.4% (range 50.0% to 96.3%). Return was highest after forearm ORIF (96.3%), tibia IMN (90.9%) and sports hernia repair (90.2%), and lowest after patellar tendon repair (50.0%). Post-surgery career length was 1.6 years after ACL reconstruction and 1.5 years after patellar tendon repair.   "limitations": "Public-source data may miss some injuries, and players who left the league for non-medical reasons may be counted as not returning. Retirement confounds the post-surgery figures, the performance score excludes offensive linemen and special teams players, and the study does not compare rehabilitation protocols.",
  "practicalImplications": "Staff can use procedure-specific return rates and career outcomes to set realistic expectations and counsel players, especially after patellar tendon repair or ACL reconstruction. A first-season dip in games and performance is expected after several procedures, and performance did not recover after ACL reconstruction or patellar tendon repair.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance staff can use the first-season performance drop after ACL reconstruction, Achilles repair, patellar tendon repair and tibia IMN to plan a graded return and monitor output after surgery. The study has no data on specific training or load, so it does not set training prescriptions.",
  "rtp": "This study is directly about return to play in professional players: 79% returned overall, 50% after patellar tendon repair, and ACL reconstruction and patellar tendon repair were followed by shorter careers and sustained performance losses. It does not compare rehabilitation protocols, so it cannot show which rehabilitation approach improves return."
 }
}

Mai,*yz§ MD, Andrew P. Alvarez,y MD, Ryan D. Freshman,y BS, Danielle S. Chun,y MD, Shobhit V. Minhas,y MD, Alpesh A. Patel,y MD, Gordon W. Nuber,y MD, and Wellington K. Hsu,y MD Investigation performed at the Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Feinberg School of Medicine, Northwestern University, Chicago, Illinois, USA Background: Injuries are inherent to the sport of American football and often require operative management. Outcomes have been reported for certain surgical procedures in professional athletes in the National Football League (NFL), but there is little infor- mation comparing the career effect of these procedures. Purpose: To catalog the postoperative outcomes of orthopaedic procedures in NFL athletes and to compare respective progno- ses and effects on careers. Study Design: Case series; Level of evidence, 4. Methods: Athletes in the NFL undergoing procedures for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears, Achilles tendon tears, patellar ten- don tears, cervical disc herniation, lumbar disc herniation, sports hernia, knee articular cartilage repair (microfracture technique), forearm fractures, tibial shaft fractures, and ankle fractures were identified through team injury reports or other public records. Game and performance statistics during the regular season were collected before and after surgery. Statistical analysis was per- formed with significance accepted as P \ .05. Results: A total of 559 NFL athletes were included. Overall, 79.4% of NFL athletes returned to play after an orthopaedic procedure. Forearm open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), sports hernia repair, and tibia intramedullary nailing (IMN) led to significantly higher return-to-play (RTP) rates (90.2%-96.3%), while patellar tendon repair led to a significantly lower rate (50%) (P \ .001). Ath- letes undergoing ACL reconstruction (ACLR), Achilles tendon repair, patellar tendon repair, and ankle fracture ORIF had significant declines in games played at 1 year and recovered to baseline at 2 to 3 years after surgery. Athletes undergoing ACLR, Achilles ten- don repair, patellar tendon repair, and tibia IMN had decreased performance in postoperative season 1. Athletes in the Achilles ten- don repair and tibia IMN cohorts recovered to baseline performance, while those in the ACLR and patellar tendon repair cohorts demonstrated sustained decreases in performance. Conclusion: ACLR, Achilles tendon repair, and patellar tendon repair have the greatest effect on NFL careers, with patellar ten- don repair faring worst with respect to the RTP rate, career length after surgery, games played, and performance at 1 year and 2 to 3 years after surgery. Downloaded from ajs.sagepub.com at OHIO STATE UNIVERSITY LIBRARY on August 21, 2016 || AJSM PreView, published on June 16, 2016 as doi:10.1177/0363546516651426 The NFL Orthopaedic Surgery Outcomes Database (NO-SOD) The Effect of Common Orthopaedic Procedures on Football Careers Harry T. Mai,*yz§ MD, Andrew P. Alvarez,y MD, Ryan D. Freshman,y BS, Danielle S. Chun,y MD, Shobhit V. Minhas,y MD, Alpesh A. Patel,y MD, Gordon W. Nuber,y MD, and Wellington K. Hsu,y MD Investigation performed at the Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Feinberg School of Medicine, Northwestern University, Chicago, Illinois, USA Background: Injuries are inherent to the sport of American football and often require operative management. Outcomes have been reported for certain surgical procedures in professional athletes in the National Football League (NFL), but there is little infor- mation comparing the career effect of these procedures. Purpose: To catalog the postoperative outcomes of orthopaedic procedures in NFL athletes and to compare respective progno- ses and effects on careers. Study Design: Case series; Level of evidence, 4. Methods: Athletes in the NFL undergoing procedures for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears, Achilles tendon tears, patellar ten- don tears, cervical disc herniation, lumbar disc herniation, sports hernia, knee articular cartilage repair (microfracture technique), forearm fractures, tibial shaft fractures, and ankle fractures were identified through team injury reports or other public records. Game and performance statistics during the regular season were collected before and after surgery. Statistical analysis was per- formed with significance accepted as P \ .05. Results: A total of 559 NFL athletes were included. Overall, 79.4% of NFL athletes returned to play after an orthopaedic procedure. Forearm open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), sports hernia repair, and tibia intramedullary nailing (IMN) led to significantly higher return-to-play (RTP) rates (90.2%-96.3%), while patellar tendon repair led to a significantly lower rate (50%) (P \ .001). Ath- letes undergoing ACL reconstruction (ACLR), Achilles tendon repair, patellar tendon repair, and ankle fracture ORIF had significant declines in games played at 1 year and recovered to baseline at 2 to 3 years after surgery. Athletes undergoing ACLR, Achilles ten- don repair, patellar tendon repair, and tibia IMN had decreased performance in postoperative season 1. Athletes in the Achilles ten- don repair and tibia IMN cohorts recovered to baseline performance, while those in the ACLR and patellar tendon repair cohorts demonstrated sustained decreases in performance. Conclusion: ACLR, Achilles tendon repair, and patellar tendon repair have the greatest effect on NFL careers, with patellar ten- don repair faring worst with respect to the RTP rate, career length after surgery, games played, and performance at 1 year and 2 to 3 years after surgery.
